  "chapter_body_excerpt": "## Shapes of practice Medical trends surrounding dian and kuang, 17th-19th century The profusion of medical works that appeared after 1650 are an irritating windfall. As medical publications boomed, vectors of knowledge transmission and the doctrinal debates that interested physicians became more intricate and numerous. It thus becomes difficult to find narrative threads to explain how Qing medical reflections on madness changed. Far too many texts were published for me to base my conclusions on comprehensive data as I tried to do for earlier periods. But the extensive array of short treatises, collections of case files, formularies, and medical primers that appeared in Qing times hint to the thinking and practice of minor physicians who made no “contributions to the development of Chinese medicine”—to borrow a phrase from a less critical historiography. These works allow us to see how much medical luminaries had in common with their less famous counterparts. I first present a few important trends in Chinese medical thinking and practice from the seventeenth to the nineteenth century. After showing that the mucus etiology remained dominant over that period, I show how resilient and ubiquitous the script of blockage of the Heart by mucus was. I map the vivid “imagination of mucus” $ ^{1} $ through which physicians—from treatise writers to village healers—continued to envision madness from the seventeenth to the nineteenth century. I then turn to a pivotal figure in eighteenth-century medicine—Ye Gui 葉桂 (1667-1746)—and to what an influential work attributed to him said about madness.
